newsitem.title: MEXICO: Zapatistas claim Mexican army ready to strike.
newsitem.headline: Zapatistas claim Mexican army ready to strike.

text.p: Mexico's Zapatista guerrillas, who are surrounded by army troops while a ceasefire holds, claim that the army is gearing up for a major offensive, a Mexican newspaper reported on Friday.
Peace talks between the predominantly Maya Indian rebels and the government broke off four months ago with little indication that the impasse can be resolved.
There has been no fighting in the three-year-old conflict since a rebel offensive in December 1994. The off-and-on peace talks began in April 1995.

Zapatista leader Subcommander Marcos said in a 21-page statement that the Mexican army has "saturated" its barracks with fresh troops in the southeastern state of Chiapas where the conflict is located, the Mexico City newspaper La Jornada reported in its Friday editions.
A buildup of airplanes and helicopters has tipped off a "surgical strike," Marcos said, according to La Jornada.

The order to attack "is in the hands of the divisional general staffs for the so-called Operation Rainbow," Marcos said. "It arrived accompanied by a presidential promise: this time there's no turning back."
A soldier in the army public relations office said early on Friday that he had no comment on the matter.
President Ernesto Zedillo assailed the Zapatistas on Thursday, accusing them of seeking to segregate Indians from the rest of Mexico, outside the jurisdiction of the government.

The Zapatistas and the government signed an agreement on Indian rights nearly a year ago, but the Zapatistas later rejected changes made in the text when the government attempted to incorporate the agreement into constitutional reforms. A separate round of talks on nationwide political reforms broke down on Sept. 2, 1996.
The Zapatistas launched their uprising on Jan. 1, 1994, leading to 11 days of fighting that killed 145 people before the government called a unilateral ceasefire.

Since then, the Zapatistas have gained international sympathy from the radical chic. Last year, figures such as film director Oliver Stone and former French First Lady Danielle Mitterrand visited the Zapatistas in Chiapas.
The Zapatistas are symbolised by Marcos, ironically not an Indian, who is always seen wearing a ski mask and smoking a pipe.
